unit.title: Passwords and login
unit.description: Hashing, salts, bcrypt and Argon2, brute force, credential stuffing, rate limiting, two-factor login, passkeys

cards.definition: Turning a password into a fixed fingerprint that cannot be reversed; the site stores the fingerprint and compares fingerprints at login.
cards.example: The database holds a long hash, never the password itself.

cards.definition: A random value added to each password before hashing, so two identical passwords give two different hashes.
cards.example: Two users with the password sunshine get unrelated hashes.

cards.definition: Hash functions designed to be slow and memory-hungry, so testing billions of guesses becomes too expensive.
cards.example: Each login takes 0.1 s to check: nothing for a user, a wall for an attacker.

cards.definition: Trying passwords one after another, often from lists of the most common ones, until one works.
cards.example: A bot tries 10,000 common passwords on the admin account.

cards.definition: Trying email and password pairs leaked from another site, betting that people reuse their passwords.
cards.example: A leak from a game forum is replayed against your shop login.

cards.definition: Capping how many attempts an account or an address may make in a given time.
cards.example: Five failed logins, then a pause of fifteen minutes.

cards.definition: Asking for a second proof besides the password: a code from an app, a passkey or a security key.
cards.example: Even with your password, the attacker lacks your phone.

cards.definition: A login based on a key stored on your device and unlocked by your fingerprint or PIN; it cannot be phished or reused.
cards.example: Sign in with your face on the phone, no password typed.

exercises.prompt: How should a site store user passwords?
choices: Hashed with Argon2 or bcrypt, with a salt
Encrypted with a key kept on the same server
In clear text, in a protected table
Encoded in base64
exercises.explain: A slow, salted hash cannot be reversed. Encryption can be undone with the key, and base64 is just an encoding anyone can decode.

exercises.prompt: A password hash can be reversed with the right key, like encryption.
exercises.explain: False: hashing is one-way. The only attack is guessing passwords and hashing each guess, which slow hashes make very expensive.

exercises.prompt: Why add a salt to each password?
choices: Same passwords get different hashes, so tables fail
It makes passwords shorter to store
It speeds up the check at each login
It encrypts the connection to the site
exercises.explain: Without a salt, one cracked hash reveals every user with the same password, and huge precomputed tables work.

exercises.prompt: Why is a single SHA-256 not enough to store passwords?
choices: It is too fast: billions of guesses a second
It can be reversed with a little effort
Its output is far too long to store
Browsers are not able to compute it
exercises.explain: SHA-256 is great for files and signatures, but its speed helps attackers. Password hashes are slow on purpose.

exercises.prompt: Attackers try email and password pairs leaked from another site on your login page. This is…
choices: Credential stuffing
Brute force on one account
XSS
SQL injection
exercises.explain: It works because many people reuse passwords. Your site was not breached, but accounts can still be taken over.

exercises.prompt: Which set of measures works best against credential stuffing?
choices: Two-factor login, rate limits, leaked-password checks
Forcing a new password every month
Longer usernames for every account
A CAPTCHA on the home page only
exercises.explain: Rate limits slow the bots, leaked-password checks remove the easy wins, and a second factor stops the rest.

exercises.prompt: Which line shows that this site stores passwords in clear text?
exercises.explain: Comparing directly means the database holds the real password. The fix: store a hash and use a verify function such as argon2 verify(hash, password).

exercises.prompt: An error message such as "no account with this email" helps attackers find valid accounts.
exercises.explain: True: it confirms which emails exist. Use one neutral message for every failed login.

exercises.prompt: What does rate limiting on a login page mean?
choices: Limiting the attempts per account or address per minute
Limiting how long a password can be
Limiting the number of users of the site
Limiting how fast HTTPS can go
exercises.explain: Without a limit, a bot can try thousands of passwords per minute. With one, brute force becomes too slow to work.

exercises.prompt: Which second factor resists phishing best?
choices: A passkey or a hardware security key
A six-digit code sent by SMS
A security question, like a pet name
A code sent to your email address
exercises.explain: A passkey is bound to the real domain, so a fake site cannot use it. Codes can be typed into a fake page and replayed.
